sources.title: ANSI/ASQ Standard Z1.4-2003 -- reproduced in an AQL reference chart, 'AQL Chart' (PDF)
sources.note: Directly fetched and read as a PDF (two pages): page 1 is the Ac/Re master table by code letter and AQL; page 2 is the Sample Size Code Letters table by lot size range and General Inspection Level I/II/III, both explicitly labeled 'SINGLE SAMPLING PLAN FOR NORMAL INSPECTION, ANSI/ASQ STANDARD Z1.4-2003.' The lot-size-to-code-letter row for '281 to 500' (F/H/J for Levels I/II/III) and the code-letter-to-sample-size rows (H=50, J=80) were both read directly off the fetched table, not paraphrased from a secondary summary. This case does not use the table's Ac/Re (accept/reject) columns for AQL>0 -- it uses a c=0 (zero acceptance number) rule instead, sourced separately as S2.

sources.claim: Zero acceptance number ('c = 0') sampling plans are a real, standard acceptance-sampling method used in regulated manufacturing (including pharmaceutical/medical device), requiring a smaller sample than the corresponding full ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 plan for a comparable assurance level, with probability of lot acceptance following (1-p)^n for true fraction defective p and sample size n
sources.value: c = 0 (accept the lot only if zero defective units are found in the sample)
sources.title: William A. Levinson, "When and How to Use Zero Acceptance Number Sampling"
sources.note: The article's full text sits behind a login wall; the publicly visible excerpt (directly fetched) confirms the article's date, author, and the specific claim that 'the zero acceptance number (c=0) sampling plan requires far less inspection than the corresponding ANSI/ASQ Z1.4' and that such plans are viable for suppliers with high quality confidence. A follow-up search independently confirmed the underlying (1-p)^n binomial relationship for c=0 plan OC curves is standard acceptance-sampling theory (referenced across multiple quality-engineering sources, including Nicholas L. Squeglia's widely-used reference text 'Zero Acceptance Number Sampling Plans,' ASQ Press) and that c=0 plans are specifically used in pharmaceutical and medical-device manufacturing for critical/major characteristics. Graded MEDIUM rather than HIGH because the exact formula was corroborated via secondary discussion of the topic rather than a single fully-rendered primary derivation page.

sources.note: Directly fetched. Attributes the 2.3% large-facility contamination sub-rate and the 'greater than $1-2 million' per-failed-batch cost figure to Beth Junker, PhD, Senior Director of Bioprocess R&D at Merck Research Laboratories, based on a worldwide survey of 145 biopharmaceutical organizations. A near-identical companion article (GenEngNews, 'Batch Failure Rates in Biomanufacturing,' same underlying survey) independently corroborates the 7% total / 2.3% large-facility-contamination figures but rendered the cost figure as '$1-2 billion' in one automated extraction pass -- BioProcess International's own directly-fetched text unambiguously reads '$1-2 million,' which is also the economically plausible reading for a single batch (a $1-2 billion single-batch loss does not match any known biologics batch scale), so the million-dollar figure from the BioProcess International fetch is the one used in this case; the discrepancy is recorded here rather than silently resolved. Graded MEDIUM (not HIGH) specifically because this is an 18-year-old (2008) figure and no more recent public equivalent with the same level of specific, named attribution was found -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md and case.md's Appendix E note on S3's age. deliverables.text: A sampling-design table for each plan identifying: the population (the full production lot), the sample (the units actually pulled for destructive testing), an individual (one tested unit and its two possible outcomes), the sample size, and the sampling method used to select which physical units are pulled -- with a written justification of why that method (not an easier one, like grabbing whichever units are most convenient to reach on the pallet) is the one the standard actually calls for.

An escape-probability calculation for each plan: using Appendix C's assumed fraction of defective units inside an out-of-spec lot, compute the probability that a fully out-of-spec lot still passes every single tested unit and ships undetected -- shown as repeated multiplication, step by step, not just a final percentage.

A full expected-cost calculation for each plan: the certain destructive-testing cost (every tested unit, at its per-unit cost from Appendix A) plus the probability-weighted cost of an undetected defect reaching the customer (Appendix C's real lot-contamination-occurrence rate, times your D2 escape probability, times Appendix C's cost of an undetected escape) -- with the arithmetic shown for every term, for both plans.

A written breakdown of D3's result: state how much of the cost difference between the two plans comes from the certain destructive-testing cost alone versus the probability-weighted risk cost, and then answer this directly -- if Lot 4471 had actually been flagged by a supplier deviation notice (Appendix C's elevated-risk scenario), would your Challenge 2 recommendation still hold? Show the recomputed D3 arithmetic for that scenario before you answer.

An original dot plot comparing the escape probability produced by at least four different candidate sample sizes (including both Lean Draw and Deep Draw), to show whether that probability drops at a steady, even rate as the sample size grows, or at some other rate.

appendices.title: The ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 Standard (Why These Are the Only Two Real Options)
Real Contamination Data and the Case's Modeling Assumptions

balance.argument_a: The Lean Draw's case is the D3 expected-cost math itself: at the industry-wide baseline contamination-occurrence rate (2.3%, sourced) and the case's stated unit-level defect-fraction assumption (MA1, 2.5%), the smaller Level II sample's much lower certain destructive-testing cost ($12,500 vs $20,000 -- a real $7,500 gap) is not offset by its higher escape probability once that probability is correctly weighted by how rarely a lot is actually bad in the first place. A's three-year... (single-lot) expected total cost comes out lower than B's by a real, moderate margin, and this holds up (never flips) across the ENTIRE possible range of MA1, not just a +/-50% flex -- verified by sensitivity_model.py's binary search across [0,1]. This is the case's central rubric trap in reverse: a Hero who assumes 'more samples must be worth it' without weighting by the real, low baseline occurrence rate will overestimate The Deep Draw's advantage.
balance.argument_b: The Deep Draw's real strength is not a cost argument under the primary metric's baseline assumptions -- it is a targeted-risk argument that becomes a genuine cost argument the moment Lot 4471 stops being an average, randomly-selected lot. Once a real, disclosed reason to suspect elevated risk exists (Appendix C's MA2, a supplier deviation notice), the Deep Draw's better escape-probability performance is no longer buying protection against a rare, industry-average risk -- it is buying protection against a meaningfully more likely event, and D4's own recomputed arithmetic shows the recommendation flips to B under that scenario. B's case is strongest for a Hero arguing from a risk-management, not a raw-expected-value, standpoint on an AVERAGE lot -- but becomes the mathematically correct expected-value choice the instant lot-specific risk information is on the table.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |total_expected_cost(A) - total_expected_cost(B)| / max(total_expected_cost(A), total_expected_cost(B)), where total_expected_cost(option) = (sample size x per-unit test cost) + [baseline lot-contamination-occurrence probability x escape probability x cost of an undetected escape], and escape probability = (1 - MA1)^(sample size). Using Appendix A/B's sourced sample sizes (50, 80) and per-unit cost ($250), Appendix C's sourced baseline occurrence rate (2.3%) and MA1 (2.5%), and the case's $1,400,000 cost-of-escape figure (chosen within Appendix C's real $1,000,000-$2,000,000 sourced range): A total = $12,500.00 + $9,080.02 = $21,580.02. B total = $20,000.00 + $4,248.40 = $24,248.40. margin = |21,580.02 - 24,248.40| / 24,248.40 = 11.0%. This is within the concept brief's 8-12% target band. See sensitivity_model.py and case.json.derived for the full reproducible arithmetic, including the D4/Twist scenario where MA2 (6%, used only for that narrower question) flips the recommendation.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fraction of individual units that are actually defective, inside a lot that IS out-of-spec
modeling_assumptions.basis: No manufacturer (Sartorius, Thermo Fisher, Cytiva, or smaller suppliers like the fictional Alden) publicly discloses a unit-level defect fraction for its own single-use consumables, and no industry body (BioPhorum/BPOG included) publishes one either -- confirmed by genuine multi-query search, see RESEARCH_LOG.md. 2.5% is set within the range of Acceptable Quality Levels the ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 standard itself is built to test major/critical characteristics against (the standard's own AQL columns span roughly 0.065% to 15%; 2.5% sits toward the tighter/more-critical end appropriate for a leak/integrity characteristic in a biologics-adjacent product).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: sensitivity_model.py's binary search across the FULL [0,1] range (not just +/-50%) found NO value of MA1 that flips the PRIMARY per-lot expected-cost recommendation -- A (The Lean Draw) wins at every fraction-defective value from 0% to 100%, because the fixed $7,500 destructive-testing cost gap between the two sample sizes is always large relative to what the escape-probability difference can be worth at the case's baseline 2.3% lot-occurrence rate. This is a genuine robustness finding for the PRIMARY metric. See MA2 below and case.json.derived.twist_flip_threshold for the DIFFERENT, much more fragile parameter that governs the D4/Twist scenario.
modeling_assumptions.flips_dilemma: primary metric: no (verified robust across the full [0,1] range by binary search).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Probability that Lot 4471 specifically is out-of-spec, GIVEN a supplier deviation notice has already flagged it (used only in the Challenge 3 / D4 Twist scenario, not the primary recommendation)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A documented supplier deviation notice on an incoming raw material is real information a quality system is required to act on (a standard real-world QC practice), but no published figure states exactly how much a specific flagged lot's risk should be assumed to rise above the sourced 2.3% industry-wide baseline (S3). 6% is a deliberately moderate multiple (about 2.6x) of that baseline -- not an extreme worst case.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: sensitivity_model.py's binary search found the D4/Twist scenario's recommendation flips from A to B at a lot-occurrence probability of only ~3.57% -- barely above the sourced 2.3% baseline, and well below the case's own stated 6% MA2 value. This means MA2 does not need to be pushed anywhere near its stated value for the flip to occur; even a modest, highly plausible elevation above the industry baseline is enough. This is the opposite finding from MA1: a small, easily-defended assumption is genuinely load-bearing here.
modeling_assumptions.flips_dilemma: D4/twist scenario: yes, at a lot-occurrence probability of approximately 3.57% -- see case.json.derived.twist_flip_threshold. The case's own stated MA2 (6%) sits above this flip point, so under the stated MA2 value the D4 scenario recommends B, not A.

derived.notes: Figures computed from sensitivity_model.py, not restated in full in case.md (facilitator-only reasoning lives in FACILITATOR.md), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record instead of drifting silently.

flip_threshold.note: sensitivity_model.py's binary search found NO value of MA1 (fraction defective within an out-of-spec lot) in [0,1] that flips the PRIMARY per-lot expected-cost recommendation (evaluate()) from A to B. A wins at every value from 0% to 100%. This is a genuine robustness finding for the PRIMARY metric specifically -- see twist_flip_threshold below for the metric where a different parameter DOES flip the answer.

twist_recompute_after_deviation_notice.note: Recomputes the per-lot expected cost for each option using MA2 (6%) as the lot-occurrence probability instead of the sourced 2.3% baseline -- the Challenge 3 (D4) / Twist scenario.

twist_flip_threshold.note: sensitivity_model.py's binary search on the lot-occurrence probability (holding MA1 fixed at 2.5%) finds the D4/Twist scenario flips from A to B at a lot-occurrence probability of approximately 3.57% -- only about 1.55x the sourced 2.3% baseline, and well below the case's own stated MA2 value of 6%. Found this way (rather than by assuming the case's stated 6% MA2 value automatically flips it) precisely because a case must verify its own twist mechanically, not just assert it.

guide_notes_arithmetic.note: Decimal-form values quoted in FACILITATOR.md's 'The margin' and 'The trap' sections, recorded here so they are checkable against a value of record (T1-14 continuity).

sensitivity_disclosure.param: MA1 (fraction defective within an out-of-spec lot)
sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No manufacturer or industry body publishes a unit-level defect fraction for single-use consumables -- this is a forecast-style assumption about an unmeasured population characteristic, not a present measurable fact. Tier 2 P5 found this parameter does NOT flip the PRIMARY per-lot verdict anywhere in the full [0,1] range (binary search), because the fixed destructive-testing cost gap between sample sizes dominates at the case's baseline 2.3% lot-occurrence rate. Disclosed as a genuine robustness finding, consistent with house doctrine that absent/uncertain data is a first-class state to be stated either way.

sensitivity_disclosure.param: lot-occurrence probability (D4/twist scenario only -- MA2 substituted for the sourced S3 baseline)
sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The sourced 2.3% baseline (S3) describes an average lot; MA2 asks what happens for a SPECIFIC, flagged lot, which is an inherently forecast-style judgment call about that one lot, not a population fact. This parameter DOES flip the narrower D4/Twist scenario, at only ~3.57% -- well below the case's own stated MA2 (6%). Disclosed explicitly and separately from MA1's robustness finding above because they are genuinely different results on different metrics, not the same finding restated -- see case.json.derived.twist_flip_threshold and FACILITATOR.md's Twist section.
